title: The quarrel of the senses
hookLine: a palm before the lips, the puff of breath in dharma, and the Upanishad's quarrel the breath wins
carry: prana: the breath every power leans on
tomorrow: a demon king asks his son what he learned at school. what did the boy say?
last: A NAME CAN BE A PRAYER.

lines: WHAT IS AIR DOING IN THE ALPHABET?
cards: Hold a palm an inch from the lips and say top. A small puff lands on the hand. Say stop, and it mostly doesn't.

English makes that puff without anyone deciding to, and it never changes what a word means. Sanskrit gives the puff a letter of its own. Which leaves one question for today: what is a little air doing in the alphabet?

teach.b: Sanskrit pairs its consonants by breath. Ka and kha. Da and dha.
The grammarians call the plain ones alpaprana, little breath, and the breathy ones mahaprana, great breath. Dharma opens on dha: DHUR-muh. And the trap for English readers: ph isn't f.
Phala, fruit, a word the Gita uses, is PUH-luh, a p with a puff. Why write breath down so carefully? The Chandogya Upanishad answers with a quarrel.
Speech, the eye, the ear and the mind each claim to be the greatest. Each one leaves the body for a while, and the body carries on: mute, or blind, or deaf, but alive.
Then breath begins to leave, and it tears the others loose, like a strong horse pulling up its tether pegs. They beg it to stay. Even speech depends on breath.

Hindus call that power prana, the life-breath, and it's why pranayama, the training of the breath, belongs to yoga and to the daily prayers of many families. A neighbor tradition says something close, in its own words.
Genesis: "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." Both put breath at the root of being alive.
The honest difference: in Genesis, God breathes it into the first human, a gift from outside.
In the Upanishad, breath is the power the body's other powers already lean on, and the story is about learning which one that is.
The h in mahaprana is that same prana, made audible.

how: Some Sanskrit teachers have students hold a hand or a slip of paper before the mouth to feel the difference between plain and breathy consonants, and chanters keep the breath in dharma, bhakti and phala.

games.q: breath in the letters — tap the pairs.
p: great breath: the one with a puff
the life-breath the senses can't do without

s: the ph in Sanskrit phala sounds like an f
it's a p with a puff of air: PUH-luh.
in the Chandogya's story, the body lives on when speech leaves
mute, but alive. only breath's leaving tears the others loose.
Genesis and the Chandogya tell the same story about breath
both put breath at the root of life; Genesis has God breathe it in, the Chandogya has the senses learn they depend on it.

games.q: a friend from church says, 'in Genesis God breathes life into the first person. is there anything like that in Hindu texts?' what's a fair answer?
o: close kin: the Chandogya puts breath at the root of life too, told as the senses' quarrel.
no: breath shows up in yoga classes, but not in the old texts.
yes, it's the same story with different names.
games.why: shared: breath at the root of being alive. different: Genesis has God breathe it into the first human; in the Chandogya the senses discover they all depend on it.

practice: With a palm near the lips, say dharma slowly and feel the puff after the d. Then lower the hand, close the eyes, and, as in pranayama, let a few breaths go slow and even, out and back, the same prana the letters are made of.
If you don't pray, simply rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: The sounds: today, with breath. Little breath and great breath, alpaprana and mahaprana: prana, the life-breath, in the letters themselves.

orig.note: Sanskrit: mahāprāṇa, great breath, the grammarians' name for a consonant with a puff of air.

carryVoice: Your line: prana, the breath every power leans on. Even the h in dharma carries it. Until tomorrow.
